clue.text: Literary group becomes ragged on the radio?

indicators.note: a radio carries only sound, so the word is judged by how it is heard, not spelt

blocks.note: cloth that becomes ragged frays at the edges

explanation.surface: A writers' circle falls apart, as reported in a radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: PHRASE and FRAYS sound identical when spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase is a small cluster of words forming a unit within a sentence, so a group in writing.

clue.text: Pressure on what could be the atom

blocks.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure
the word 'the' is the definite article in grammar

explanation.surface: A physicist speculates on what pressure does to an atom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the atom' looks like one phrase, but 'the' is the example word being described and 'atom' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom is one example of a tiny unit of matter, the kind physicists class as a particle.

clue.text: Painting of kettle and cake

blocks.note: a kettle that sings when boiling is a whistler; the possessive S joins it
to cake something is to smother it, read here as S plus MOTHER

explanation.surface: A still-life painting showing a kettle beside a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive S moves across the word break, so 'cake' supplies the verb smother. The answer is the famous 1871 portrait by James McNeill Whistler.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the popular title of Whistler's 1871 portrait of his elderly mother seated in profile, a celebrated artwork.

clue.text: Pleat pinned by boy, firmly attached

indicators.note: something pinned by another thing is held in place between it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: a boy in relation to his parents is a son
a tuck is a fold sewn into fabric, like a pleat

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's pleat is held in place with a pin by a young lad.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stuck on has been glued or fixed to a surface so it stays secure.

clue.text: Cheese on conventional board game property

blocks.note: Red Leicester is an English cheese named after the county
square is slang for old-fashioned or conventional

explanation.surface: Someone lays cheese on a traditional game board.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second. Leicester Square is a property on the British Monopoly board, and a real square in London's West End.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the purchasable sites in the London edition of Monopoly, the property-trading game.

clue.text: Repeated words making chap with skill uplifted

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting something up turns it to read from the bottom upward

blocks.note: a chap is a man
art means a skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A man with a talent is lifted in spirit by chanting the same words.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the skill word turns around; the chap stays as he is.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantra is a word or phrase chanted over and over, especially in meditation.

clue.text: OT character in trouble, vindicated

indicators.note: in tells the solver the letters sit inside the words that follow

blocks.note: the end of trouble runs into the start of vindicated

explanation.surface: A figure from the Old Testament gets into difficulty and is later cleared.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters straddle the comma: troub-LE, VI-ndicated.
explanation.definitionFit: Levi, third son of Jacob and founder of the Levite tribe, appears in the Old Testament, abbreviated OT.

clue.text: Which person comes to a stop?

blocks.note: who asks which person
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about who is going to halt.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoa is the command to halt, originally shouted to horses, so it serves as the imperative 'stop!'.

clue.text: Winner smashed

blocks.note: first meaning: a big success
second meaning: struck hard, the past tense of the verb

explanation.surface: A champion has been beaten or wrecked.
explanation.definitionFit: A hit is a popular success, and to hit something is to strike it, past tense unchanged.

clue.text: Ed Banks dead happy!

indicators.note: banks line both sides of a river, so the name sits on either side of the next word

blocks.note: taken as written, split to sit at both ends
the late someone is someone who has died

explanation.surface: Someone called Ed Banks is extremely pleased.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ed Banks' reads as a full name, but Banks is the instruction for Ed to sit on both sides. 'Dead happy' is also informal for very happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Elated means full of joy and excitement, a stronger word for glad.

clue.text: Group granny knocked over in French city

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up the other way round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a set is a group of things
nan is an informal word for grandmother

explanation.surface: A gang knocks down an old woman while visiting France.
explanation.walkthrough: SET and NAN together are read backwards; NAN reads the same either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a large port city on the Loire in western France.

clue.text: Tip back mixed drink

blocks.note: to cock is to tilt, as in cocking one's head
the tail is at the back end

explanation.surface: A barman is told to tilt a blended drink backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip back' looks like one instruction, but it is two separate words, each giving a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A cocktail is an alcoholic drink made by combining spirits with other ingredients.

clue.text: Remarkably hip soul, me: accent that’s fine and clipped

indicators.note: remarkably suggests something done in an unusual way, so the letters are rearranged out of their usual order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of these words are used

explanation.surface: A trendy soul singer boasts of a refined, clipped way of speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine and clipped' sounds like an accent, but it describes a thin, neatly trimmed line of facial hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A pencil moustache is a very thin, closely trimmed strip of hair above the upper lip.

clue.text: Weed with no name, ultimately

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only each word's closing letter is kept

blocks.note: the final letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A wild plant nobody has named in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To weed a bed is to remove unwanted plants, which is the job of a hoe, used here as a verb.

clue.text: ‘Island‘ composed by Gershwin?

blocks.note: composed means put together or made
Ira Gershwin was the lyricist brother of George Gershwin

explanation.surface: A song called 'Island' written by one of the Gershwin brothers.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits Gershwin could be George or Ira; only Ira fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Madeira is a Portuguese island in the Atlantic, off the coast of north-west Africa.

clue.text: Show what goes over one’s ‘ead?

indicators.note: the apostrophe in this word marks a dropped opening letter, telling the solver to drop the same letter from the answer

blocks.note: hair grows on top of the head

explanation.surface: A question about what passes over someone's head, spoken in a dropped-aitch accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ead is head said with the H dropped, as in a Cockney accent, so HAIR is said the same way: 'AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: To air a view or a programme is to make it public or broadcast it, so to display it.

clue.text: Spirit that is observed on board ship in pictures

indicators.note: being on board a vessel means being inside it, so the words go within the outer letters

blocks.note: SS stands for steamship
an elf is a sprite or small spirit
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A ghost seen aboard a ship turns up in photographs.
explanation.definitionFit: Selfies are photographs people take of themselves, usually with a phone.

clue.text: Deal with eccentric king or queen, say

blocks.note: to face a problem is to deal with it
a card is an amusingly odd person

explanation.surface: Handling an odd monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deal' and 'king or queen' suggest cards from the start, but 'Deal with' is a verb meaning confront.
explanation.definitionFit: In a deck, the king, queen and jack are the court cards that carry pictures of figures.

clue.text: Train due, ETA adjusted to accommodate first of cancellations

indicators.note: adjusted means altered, so these letters are put into a different order
to accommodate a guest is to take them in, so one piece goes inside the other
first of keeps only the opening letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: the letters of both words, to be rearranged
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A train due in has its expected time of arrival changed because of cancellations.
explanation.walkthrough: ETA is estimated time of arrival. 'Train' looks like the railway subject, but it is the verb meaning teach.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone is to teach and instruct them, which is to educate.

clue.text: Old mechanism in car’s weird: scheme failing

indicators.note: something failing is breaking down, so the letters collapse into a new order

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: A vintage car breaks down because of a strange failed scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weird' also looks like an anagram signal, but it is part of the letters; 'failing' does that job.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archimedes screw is an ancient device for lifting water, a spiral turning in a tube.

clue.text: Little pig, quite possibly, in play?

blocks.note: first meaning, playful: ham with the diminutive ending -let, as in piglet, would be a small ham
second meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Danish prince

explanation.surface: A small pig appearing in a stage show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite possibly' and the question mark admit the first meaning is invented, building a word from ham and the diminutive -let.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is Shakespeare's tragedy, and the -let ending makes a small version of something, here ham.

clue.text: Say, I’m so amazing — is that it?

definitions.text: Say, I’m so amazing — is that it?

indicators.note: amazing hints at something astonishing that jumbles expectations, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: e.g. is short for for example, used where one might say 'say'
the letters of these two words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone boasting how wonderful they are is asked if this is vanity.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: boasting 'I'm so amazing' is exactly the self-regard it names.
explanation.definitionFit: Egoism is excessive self-interest and self-regard, of the kind voiced by a person praising themselves.

clue.text: Surface that’s huge covering borders in Egypt

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it, so one piece goes outside the other
borders are the edges, so only the outermost letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: cosmic means vast, on the scale of the universe
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A vast area spreading over the frontiers of Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surface' looks like a noun, but it is the adjective meaning superficial.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmetic changes are superficial ones affecting only appearance, not substance.

clue.text: Roof off chicken houses — oh dear

indicators.note: in a down clue the roof is the top, so taking it off removes the opening letter

blocks.note: hens are kept in coops

explanation.surface: The roof has blown off the henhouses, and someone sighs at the damage.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations of mild dismay uttered after a small accident or mistake.

clue.text: Not okay being warm, possibly?

blocks.note: first meaning: unfashionable or unacceptable
second meaning, playful: something ..., not cold, could be warm

explanation.surface: Is it unacceptable to be feeling warm?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' and the question mark flag the literal reading of not cool in temperature.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncool is slang for unfashionable or unacceptable, and literally 'not cool' could mean warm.

clue.text: Field something round

blocks.note: first meaning: an area of activity or expertise
second meaning: a ball-shaped solid

explanation.definitionFit: A sphere is a domain of influence or interest, and also a perfectly round three-dimensional shape.

clue.text: Sailor in fact a rating

indicators.note: in tells the solver the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: spans the end of fact, the word a, and the start of rating

explanation.surface: A seaman who is in reality only a low-ranking crewman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rating' is itself naval slang for an ordinary sailor, tempting the solver to look for a definition there.
explanation.definitionFit: Tar, from tarpaulin, is old informal slang for a seaman.

clue.text: Wine took off

blocks.note: first meaning: pink wine, written rosé
second meaning: went up, the past tense of rise

explanation.surface: Someone's wine sales soared.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosé is a pink wine, accent dropped in the grid, and rose is the past of rise, meaning ascended.
